title: Iterative divide off ALU critical path
motivation: The baseline timing report shows the critical path running through the forwarding logic into the EX-stage ALU, with an extremely low 5.442 MHz Fmax. The ALU currently contains fully combinational RV32M multiply, divide, and remainder logic in the same output mux used by ordinary ADD/address operations, so the FPGA timing engine must close paths through very deep arithmetic even when CoreMark mostly needs simple integer and memory-address operations.

This should substantially improve Fmax on Tang Nano 20K; any extra cycles should be negligible unless the workload is division-heavy.

title: Move RV32M ops into a multi-cycle execute unit
motivation:
The baseline timing path is dominated by the EX-stage cone from forwarding
through the combinational ALU, and the current ALU computes multiply,
divide, and remainder hardware in the same always_comb block as every
single-cycle integer op. On Tang Nano 20K this creates a very deep LUT/DSP
path that caps Fmax around 5.4 MHz, far below the target and far more costly
than a few extra cycles on infrequent M-extension instructions.

algebraic substitutes so the formal depth remains tractable. Removing
combinational multiply/divide/remainder from the always-active ALU should
collapse the worst path to forwarding plus a simple ALU/branch cone, giving a
large Fmax increase with limited CoreMark IPC loss.

title: Tiny BHT next-PC predictor
motivation: The current pipeline always fetches pc+4 and resolves every taken branch or jump in EX, so tight CoreMark loops pay a two-instruction flush on each taken back edge. CoreMark's hot code has many direct loop branches and unconditional JAL control transfers whose targets are available from the fetched instruction bits, making them good candidates for a very small predictor that improves iterations per cycle without touching the memory contract.

title: Dedicated load-store address adder
motivation:
After DIV/REM moved out of the combinational ALU, the remaining best-known
timing path is much shorter but still runs from the ID/regfile side through
EX and the ALU into the data-memory address path. CoreMark has frequent
loads and stores, so the effective-address calculation is both hot and
timing-sensitive. Today those addresses use the full RV32IM ALU result mux,
even though a memory address only needs rs1 plus the sign-extended immediate.

title: Retimed two-stage execute path
motivation:
The current champion removed the divider from the one-cycle ALU, but the
reported worst path still runs through the register-file/forwarding path into
the execute ALU before reaching the next timed boundary. CoreMark is now more
likely limited by Fmax than by rare RV32M divide latency, so a structural
retiming of the hot execute cone is the most promising remaining angle in
this slot.

title: Tagged BTB without IF decode
motivation:
The current champion still pays the full taken-control penalty because fetch
always advances to pc+4 and EX later redirects on taken branches and jumps.
The previous predictor attempt proved there is CoreMark cycle-count upside,
but it collapsed Fmax by decoding io_imemData and forming branch/JAL targets
directly in the fetch PC-update cone. A predictor that learns targets after
EX resolution and only indexes by PC in IF should recover hot loop and direct
jump penalties while staying off the existing forwarding/ALU critical path.

title: Tighter load-use hazard gating
motivation:
The current best core already removed the dominant DIV/REM cone, and recent
experiments show that larger predictor and execute-retiming ideas can add
more timing risk than CoreMark reward. The remaining control logic still
treats the next instruction's raw rs1 and rs2 bit fields as real operands
for every opcode, and it derives those fields through the IF-stage
flush/redirect NOP mux. That can create unnecessary one-cycle load-use
bubbles on I-type, load, upper-immediate, jump, fence, or system
instructions whose immediate bits happen to match a preceding load's rd,
and it leaves a timing arc from EX redirect through IF into the hazard
unit and back to the ID/EX register controls.

title: Decoupled sequential fetch queue
motivation:
The current core exposes a combinational IF/ID payload and injects a frontend
bubble every time the random instruction bus deasserts io_imemReady. During
dmem stalls, load-use bubbles, divider stalls, and redirect recovery, the
backend often cannot consume an instruction, but the existing PC path simply
holds instead of using ready imem cycles to fetch ahead. Prior predictor
attempts recovered some CoreMark cycles but lost too much Fmax by adding
target lookup and next-PC muxing on the fetch path; a purely sequential
fetch buffer attacks the stall overlap opportunity without predicting
control flow.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the combinational IF/ID handoff with a two-entry sequential fetch
queue. The fetch side keeps an independent fetch_pc and pushes pc/instr

decode side pops one entry only when ID is allowed to advance. Redirects
from EX flush the queue and restart fetch_pc at the resolved target; there
is no BHT, BTB, or instruction-immediate decode in IF. This should let dmem
stalls, load-use bubbles, divider holds, and taken-branch bubbles prefill
one or two following instructions, so later random i-stalls are absorbed by
the queue instead of becoming CoreMark bubbles. Registering the IF/ID
boundary should also reduce the u_if/u_hazard/u_id feedback path seen in
recent timing reports, while preserving the existing single-retire RVFI
contract and EX-stage branch semantics.

motivation:
The current single-issue pipeline still pays a redirect bubble on every
taken direct branch and JAL because fetch always advances to pc+4 until EX
resolves control flow. Prior BHT and BTB attempts showed that learned state
on the fetch next-PC path costs too much Fmax on Tang Nano 20K, but CoreMark
loop back edges are mostly statically identifiable from the branch immediate
sign bit.

the recurring CoreMark loop-back bubble with much less LUT, FF, and timing
cost than a BHT/BTB.

motivation:
The current champion is mostly Fmax-limited after DIV/REM were removed from
the common ALU path, and the failed predictor/fetch-queue attempts show that
frontend speculation is too expensive for this FPGA target. One remaining
structural source of lost CoreMark cycles is that every store in MEM freezes
the whole in-order pipeline whenever the randomized dmem bus deasserts
ready, even though stores produce no register result.

title: Tiny return-stack predictor
motivation:
The prior predictor attempts all tried to steer the next fetch for direct
branches or BTB hits and paid for that choice on the Tang Nano 20K fetch
timing path. CoreMark still contains call/return control flow, and every
JALR return currently behaves like any other jump: fetch goes to pc+4 until
EX resolves the real target and flushes the wrong-path instruction.

A return-address stack is a more specialized predictor with a much smaller
IF cost than a direct branch predictor. The predicted target is already a
registered stack top, so IF only needs a canonical-return recognizer and a
mux, not an immediate target adder, BHT/BTB table lookup, or tag compare.

title: Two-entry loop target cache
motivation:
Prior predictor attempts proved that CoreMark has roughly 5-6% cycle-count
upside from avoiding recurring taken-control redirects, but they lost more
Fmax than they gained because instruction decode, target adders, table
lookup, or RAS update logic landed on the fetch next-PC path. The most
promising remaining predictor angle is therefore a much smaller learned
target structure that specializes in loop back edges and avoids any
combinational update path from EX back into IF.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a two-entry loop target cache that allocates only when EX resolves a
taken direct backward branch or direct JAL with a low code-space target.
Each entry stores a small partial PC tag and a full resolved target. IF
compares the current PC against the two registered tags and, on a hit,
predicts the registered target; otherwise it fetches pc+4 exactly as today.
Updates happen only in clocked state, with no same-cycle write-through from
EX into the IF prediction result. The instruction carries predicted-taken
and predicted-target metadata to EX, which redirects only when the predicted
next PC differs from the resolved next PC; partial-tag aliases and loop exits

fetch timing cost than the previous BHT, BTB, static immediate predictor, or
RAS designs: no IF instruction decode, no IF target adder, no saturating
counters, no RAM read mux, and no EX-update bypass through the predictor.

flushing the predicted-target instruction. This keeps all learned state out

title: Sideband low dmem address path
motivation:
The current best core is Fmax-limited by paths that reach the data-memory
RAM address after passing through the forwarded operand and EX ALU cone.
Prior address-adder attempts regressed because they duplicated a full
effective-address adder and then added result-selection logic on the hot
EX/MEM path. The FPGA wrapper, however, indexes dmem only with
io_dmemAddr[12:2], while byte-lane selection and RVFI still need the full
architectural address to remain exact.

Add a narrow sideband effective-address calculation for memory operations:

implementation_notes:
Sideband low dmem address path
==============================

Changed the EX/MEM payload to carry `mem_addr_low[12:0]`, mirrored in both
`core_pkg.sv` and `00_core_pkg.sv`.

`ex_stage.sv` now computes `rs1[12:0] + imm[12:0]` after the existing
forwarding muxes and registers it with the EX/MEM payload. The full ALU result
path is unchanged and still feeds architectural writeback, full address high
bits, branch/jump behavior, and RVFI-visible ALU state.

`mem_stage.sv` now forms the data-memory address from
`{alu_result[31:13], mem_addr_low}` and uses the sideband low bits for byte
masks, misalignment checks, load extraction, and aligned RVFI memory address
low bits. Store data replication and MEM/WB retirement behavior are unchanged.

Deviations: none from the hypothesis beyond leaving the sideband populated for
all non-DIV EX operations; it is only consumed when memory controls are active.
DIV/REM captures write zero into the sideband because they are never memory
operations.

Concerns: this relies on the invariant that RV32I load/store effective
addresses are `rs1 + imm`, which the existing decoder/ALU path already uses.
The combined address should therefore be bit-exact with the full ALU result,
while giving the timed low dmem index a narrower adder path.

title: Corrected two-stage execute retime
motivation: The current champion is still limited by the register/forwarding-to-ALU/data-memory timing cone after DIV/REM were removed from the one-cycle ALU. Most later structural work added frontend prediction, queues, or LSU replay muxes and lost Fmax or disturbed block-RAM inference. The one structural idea that directly attacks the hot execute cone, splitting EX into two timed stages, was not evaluated for fitness because wrong-path instructions already sitting in the new execute register were not killed on redirects.

hypothesis.motivation: The current champion is still limited by the register/forwarding-to-ALU/data-memory timing cone after DIV/REM were removed from the one-cycle ALU. Most later structural work added frontend prediction, queues, or LSU replay muxes and lost Fmax or disturbed block-RAM inference. The one structural idea that directly attacks the hot execute cone, splitting EX into two timed stages, was not evaluated for fitness because wrong-path instructions already sitting in the new execute register were not killed on redirects.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Reintroduce a two-stage execute pipeline, but make precise valid/kill behavior the first-class design constraint. EX1 should do forwarding selection and latch the chosen operands, immediate, PC, instruction, decoded control, and store data. EX2 should contain the ALU, one-cycle multiplier, branch/jump target calculation, misalignment checks, iterative divider capture, and the existing EX/MEM register update.

On every taken branch, jump, misprediction-equivalent redirect, illegal target trap, or reset/flush event, the control logic must kill both younger frontend instructions and any wrong-path payload already resident in the EX1/EX2 register. Dmem stalls and divider stalls must hold the correct stage contents rather than replaying or dropping requests. Forwarding should target EX1 from the registered EX2/MEM result and MEM/WB result; load-use logic should account for the extra stage so dependent loads still wait for real load data.

This pays one additional branch/jump recovery cycle, but CoreMark's present score appears Fmax-limited and prior predictor/queue attempts suggest the fetch side is the wrong place to spend logic. If the execute split raises Fmax by about 15% while keeping steady-state throughput at one instruction per cycle for independent ALU and memory operations, it can clear the 4.6% replacement threshold even with modest extra control-flow bubbles.

title: Tiny loop replay predictor
motivation:
Prior predictor attempts recovered roughly five to six percent of CoreMark
cycles, but each lost more Fmax than it gained by putting instruction decode,
tag lookup, target comparison, or a target mux on the IF next-PC path. The
current champion is already Fmax-sensitive, so another general branch
predictor is unlikely to clear the acceptance threshold.

CoreMark also runs with about twenty-two percent random instruction-memory
stalls. A predictor that recognizes a hot short loop and locally replays its
instruction body can attack both taken-branch bubbles and repeated imem
stalls, while avoiding arbitrary IF target generation.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a tiny eight-instruction loop replay predictor for short direct backward
loops. During normal fetch, keep a rolling history of the most recent valid
aligned instructions and PCs. When EX resolves a taken direct backward
conditional branch whose target and contiguous body are still in that
history, allocate a replay entry containing the loop body, target PC, branch
PC, and loop length.

On later visits to the loop target, IF enters replay mode and feeds ID from
the registered loop body using a small counter instead of imemData. The loop
branch at the end is predicted taken by resetting the replay counter to the
first body instruction; EX validates the real outcome and recovers to pc+4
on loop exit or any mismatch. During replay, imemReady is ignored for the
buffered instructions, and io_imemAddr can stay on a simple registered
fall-through or prefetch address rather than selecting a learned target.

This is a predictor, but it is deliberately not another BHT/BTB/RAS in the
failed style: the hot prediction is "continue/restart this validated local
loop stream", not "choose an arbitrary target in IF". Correct hot loops
should avoid recurring redirect bubbles and most instruction-bus stalls
inside the body; aliases, exits, interrupts of replay by dmem/divider stalls,
and unsupported loop shapes fall back to the existing precise EX redirect
behavior without weakening RVFI, trap, or memory invariants.

motivation:
The current champion's worst path is now very local: it starts at the
EX1/EX2 control bit `is_auipc`, passes through the EX-stage ALU operand
mux and adder, and reaches the data-memory side. Prior memory-address
sidebands and dedicated address adders regressed because they duplicated
address logic or added selectors around the RAM-facing path. The better
micro-optimization is to keep the successful two-stage execute topology
but remove the remaining EX2 operand-selection muxes from the hot ALU cone.

CoreMark cycles. The existing rs1/rs2 payload fields should remain intact
for branch compares, JALR target calculation, divider operands, store data,
forwarding visibility, and RVFI reporting; only the ALU input path is
retimed.

title: IDEX early backedge predictor
motivation:
The current champion gained Fmax by splitting execute, but it now resolves
taken branches and jumps one stage later, so CoreMark loop backedges pay an
enlarged redirect penalty. Prior predictor attempts show that IF-side BHT,
BTB, RAS, decode feedback, and loop-replay machinery lose too much timing
when they decode io_imemData or select arbitrary learned targets on the
fetch PC path. A predictor that acts only from the already-registered ID/EX
branch metadata can recover part of the control penalty while keeping IF
nearly as simple as the champion.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a late static control predictor that fires when a valid ID/EX
instruction is actually allowed to enter EX1. For direct JAL, predict taken
to pc+imm. For conditional branches with a negative B-immediate, predict
taken to pc+imm; keep forward branches and JALR on the existing resolved
EX2 redirect path. Carry predicted_taken and predicted_target into the

control and immediate already sitting in ID/EX, adds no instruction-memory
decode, no tag table, and no multi-target lookup in IF. The only new PC
choice is an early redirect through the existing redirect-priority PC update
path, so Fmax risk should be much lower than the failed fetch predictors.
Hot CoreMark loops should save one redirect bubble per taken backedge, while
the occasional loop exit pays one corrective redirect.

through the pipe. The current champion instead wins by retiming local
